blocks.instruction: Leia o texto e escolha a alternativa correta. Algumas perguntas pedem inferência — a resposta não está escrita com todas as letras.
blocks.passage:
Please and sorry do heavy lifting in British offices — far more than they appear to. "Sorry to bother you" at the start of a request is not really an apology; it is the British way of saying: this is important enough that I am using your time, and I respect that. "If you have a moment" plays a similar role. Together, they open almost any conversation.

Overusing them can sound weak, but not using them at all can sound cold — especially to older or more traditional colleagues. The balance, for most British offices, is simple: say please and sorry more than you think you need to, but let your actual request stand clear and confident underneath.

Soft packaging, firm content. That is the British request in one line.

items.q: According to the text, what is "Sorry to bother you" really doing?
options: Signalling respect for the other person's time
items.why: "it is the British way of saying… I am using your time, and I respect that." — não é uma desculpa de verdade.

items.q: What is the risk of not using please and sorry at all?
items.why: "not using them at all can sound cold — especially to older or more traditional colleagues."

items.q: "Soft packaging, firm content" means the request should be…
options: short and stripped of all courtesy
polite in tone but clear and confident underneath
items.why: É o resumo da lição: embalagem suave, conteúdo firme.

items.q: The author would most likely DISAGREE with which statement?
options: "If you have a moment" helps open a conversation.
Politeness and a clear request can coexist.
Being too polite risks sounding weak, so drop please and sorry to stay firm.
items.why: Inferência: o texto pede as duas coisas juntas — cortesia por fora e firmeza por dentro —, não abrir mão de please e sorry.

items.q: The text suggests that, for a British reader, a message with no please or sorry would most likely feel…
items.why: Inferência: se a ausência soa "cold", o leitor britânico tende a sentir o texto seco/rude.

blocks.instruction: Ouça Charlotte ajudando um novo colega a reescrever um e-mail que ficou direto demais. Responda sem ler a transcrição — ela só aparece depois de corrigir.

audio.text:
Okay, let's look at your email together. The content is fine — you are asking the client to send the signed contract by Friday. That's a perfectly reasonable request. The problem is the wording. Right now it reads: "Send me the signed contract by Friday." To a British client, that lands as an order, not a request.

Here's what I'd do. Open with something soft — "Sorry to bother you" or "I hope you're well." Then frame the ask indirectly: instead of "Send me the contract," try "Would it be possible to send the signed contract by Friday?" or "Could you possibly get it back to us before the weekend?" Same deadline, same firmness — just wrapped more gently.

And don't worry about sounding too polite. In Portuguese this version might feel almost excessive, but in British English it's exactly right. My rule is simple: the more senior the reader, the more indirect the language. For a junior colleague you can be a bit more direct; for a client director, soften it further.

Read it back once you've changed it. If it still feels a little too polite to you, it's probably perfect.
audio.label: Ouça quantas vezes precisar. A transcrição aparece depois de corrigir.

items.q: What does Charlotte say is actually wrong with the email?
items.why: "The content is fine… The problem is the wording."

items.q: How does "Send me the signed contract by Friday" land with a British client?
options: As an order, not a request
items.why: "it lands as an order, not a request."

items.q: What is Charlotte's rule about indirectness?
options: Always use the same tone for everyone
Be more direct with clients than with colleagues
The more senior the reader, the more indirect the language
items.why: "the more senior the reader, the more indirect the language."

items.q: When Charlotte says "Same deadline, same firmness — just wrapped more gently," she implies that indirect framing…
options: keeps the request firm while softening the tone
removes the deadline to avoid pressure
items.why: Inferência: a exigência continua a mesma; só a embalagem muda — soft packaging, firm content.

items.q: Why does Charlotte say that if it "still feels a little too polite," it's probably perfect?
options: Because British norms expect more politeness than Portuguese ones
Because the client dislikes short emails
Because the new colleague writes badly
Because politeness hides the real deadline
items.why: Inferência: o que soa "educado demais" para quem pensa em português costuma ser o tom certo em inglês britânico.

blocks.instruction: O vocabulário da lição aparece aqui em frases novas. Escolha o sentido ou a palavra que cabe no contexto.

items.q: "In British emails, please and sorry do a lot of heavy lifting." Heavy lifting means…
items.why: Heavy lifting = o trabalho pesado, a parte que realmente sustenta a mensagem.

items.q: "Sorry to bother you, but could we review the numbers?" To bother someone is to…
items.why: To bother = incomodar, tomar o tempo/atenção da pessoa.

items.q: Choose the correct word: "Saying sorry too often can start to ___ the word and make you sound unsure."
items.why: To overuse = usar demais, ao ponto de esvaziar o efeito.

items.q: "A good client email is soft packaging with firm content." This contrast means…
options: a formal greeting with no deadline
a warm tone carrying a clear, confident request
a short message with no request
a strict tone with a vague request
items.why: Soft packaging = embalagem suave; firm content = conteúdo firme. Educado por fora, claro por dentro.

items.q: "Traditional colleagues can find a request with no courtesy quite cold." Here, cold means…
items.why: Cold = frio, distante — o oposto do tom cordial que os britânicos esperam.

blocks.instruction: Expressões e phrasal verbs que aparecem quando ajustamos o tom de um e-mail. Escolha o sentido no contexto.

items.q: "Would it be possible to send the file by Friday?" This phrasing is used to…
options: make a request sound more polite and indirect
ask whether the task is technically achievable only
items.why: "Would it be possible…?" é uma forma indireta e educada de pedir — mais suave que "Can you…?".

items.q: "Could you possibly get it back to us before the weekend?" Adding "possibly" mainly…
options: signals respect for the reader's time
items.why: "Could you possibly…?" sinaliza que você reconhece que está pedindo um favor e respeita o tempo do outro.

items.q: "The client still has to sign off on the contract." To sign off on means to…
items.why: Sign off on = aprovar formalmente, dar o aval final.

items.q: "Two colleagues pushed back on the blunt wording." They…
items.why: Push back on = resistir, discordar — sem necessariamente rejeitar de vez.

items.q: "We agreed to soften the emails, but the team never followed through." They…
options: failed to carry the change to completion
items.why: Follow through = levar até o fim aquilo que foi combinado.
